description:
Somos un equipo interdisciplinario conformado por 6 integrantes: 3 estudiantes de Kinesiología y 3 estudiantes de Desarrollo de Software.
Nuestro grupo surge de la combinación de conocimientos del área de la salud y la tecnología, con el objetivo de desarrollar un software destinado al monitoreo de la salud de los astronautas durante sus misiones espaciales.
summary:
Kinesoft is a web-based crew medical assistant developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to monitor astronaut health during long-duration missions. From the first day in microgravity, the human body changes: fluids shift toward the head, bones lose mineral density, muscles atrophy and the cardiovascular system deconditions. Added to radiation, isolation and a closed cabin, these risks become critical when the crew is too far from Earth for a rapid medical evacuation.

To address this challenge, we built a system that follows 114 physiological parameters across 38 anatomical zones, covering bones, muscles, organs and the mind, in three environments: the ISS, Mars transit and an Artemis lunar base. Data comes from the INTI suit’s biosensors (EEG, EMG, PPG and pulse oximetry), daily logs or CSV files. A physiological engine models microgravity effects by mission day, and a clinical triage compares each value with the astronaut’s own preflight baseline, classifying it as normal, caution or alert.

This matters because communication delays of up to 22 minutes make crew autonomy essential. Kinesoft detects risks early, suggests targeted exercise countermeasures and prepares a reconditioning plan for the return to Earth gravity, so that every crew member returns home as healthy as they left.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Kinesoft is a web-based crew medical assistant for long-duration spaceflight. It monitors the health of every crew member throughout the mission, tracking 114 clinical parameters across 38 anatomical zones in four layers: bones, muscles, organs and mind and performance. Examples include relative bone mineral density and calcaneal T-score, muscle thickness, stiffness and strength, cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure, EEG band power, LVEF, resting heart rate, FVC, SpO₂, urinary calcium, glucose, sleep, working memory, reaction time and mood.

The app works in three steps:

  1. Data input. Data comes from three sources: a daily clinical log, CSV import, and a simulated biosensor suit (INTI suit) with EEG, EMG, PPG, pulse oximetry, pupil cameras, core temperature and radiation sensors.
  2. Clinical engine. A physiological engine models how each parameter drifts in microgravity, based on mission day, gravity level and exercise adherence. It covers three mission environments: the ISS, a Mars transit and an Artemis lunar base. It compares each value with the crew member’s Earth baseline and classifies it as normal, caution or alert. It also flags cross-system patterns, such as sleep deficit combined with cognitive decline, or possible cabin hypercapnia.
  3. Response. Results appear on an interactive anatomical figure, in trend charts and as alerts. The app then builds a daily exercise prescription ranked by the status of each body zone.

The crew can also ask questions of INTI, our chat assistant. Its name means “sun” in Quechua, after the Inca sun deity. INTI answers health-status questions by voice or text, explains every parameter and its thresholds, and guides onboard protocols such as CPR, motion sickness and low back pain.

What benefits does it offer?

  • Early warning: triage flags deviations before they become clinically significant.
  • Each crew member is compared with their own preflight baseline.
  • One whole-body view brings together musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, neurological, respiratory, renal, metabolic and behavioral data.
  • Countermeasures are targeted to the zones that need them.
  • The crew gains clinical autonomy when communication with Earth is delayed, by up to 22 minutes on a Mars transit.

What is the intended impact?
Our goal is that every crew member returns home as healthy as they left. Kinesoft addresses the five hazards of NASA’s Human Research Program: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity and hostile closed environments. It helps detect bone loss, muscle atrophy and fatigue early, supports decisions far from Earth, and prepares the crew for return to 1 g with a reconditioning plan. In the future, simulated values could be replaced with real suit sensors and validated with flight data for Artemis and Mars missions.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Front end: HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks. About 40 scripts.
  • Graphics: hand-written SVG for the anatomy, charts and HUD, and Canvas 2D for the animated space background.
  • Browser APIs: localStorage, the Web Speech API, MutationObserver, Blob, FileReader and DOMParser, the dialog element and matchMedia.
  • Our own logic, with no external services: the clinical engine, an offline English/Spanish translator, and INTI, which is rule-based and uses no external AI.
  • Development tools: Python 3 for a single-file build, Node.js 22 for automated tests, Prettier, ESLint and Playwright.
  • Data formats: CSV and JSON.
  • Hosting: Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages.
  • Hardware concept: the suit’s sensor network is designed around an ESP32 with Bluetooth Low Energy.
  • Writing and coding support: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Syren.

How is your project creative?
Kinesoft turns complex clinical data into an interactive body map that anyone on the crew can read through color coding. It combines a physiological simulation, a futuristic biosensor suit with a helmet HUD, and a bilingual voice assistant whose name honors Andean culture. It also designs exercise countermeasures from the status of each body zone, including a weighted-helmet neck training routine and a return-to-gravity plan.

What factors did your team consider?

  • NASA’s five human spaceflight hazards and communication delays.
  • Working offline and serverless, so the app runs in any browser with no installation.
  • Data privacy: data stays on the device.
  • Usability under stress: touch-based navigation, color coding plus text labels, voice, and English and Spanish.
  • Accessibility: reduced-motion support and light and dark themes.
  • Clinical safety: INTI does not replace the flight surgeon or mission control.
  • Scientific grounding in references on physiology, anatomy, neuroanatomy, respiratory physiology, semiology and physical rehabilitation.
